subject: ela
cluster: Range of reading and level of text complexity

items.prompt:
Read the story below.

Anna and her grandmother baked bread every Sunday. Grandma never used a measuring cup. She just knew. 'How do you know how much to put in?' asked Anna. Grandma smiled. 'My hands remember,' she said. Anna watched her grandmother's hands move without hesitating. One day, she thought, her hands would remember too.

What is the main idea of this story? Use one detail from the text to support your answer.
items.answer: The main idea is that some knowledge is passed down through practice and experience, not just by following rules or measurements. The detail that supports this is Grandma's hands 'remember' how to make bread without measuring cups, and Anna hopes that one day her hands will too. This shows a tradition being passed from grandmother to grandchild through doing, not explaining.

steps: Ask: what is the most important idea the whole story is about?
The story is about two things happening together: baking and the passing of skill from grandmother to granddaughter.
Key detail: Grandma says 'my hands remember' — knowledge lives in the body, not in instructions.
Anna's thought at the end shows she understands this and wants to carry it on.
Main idea: some knowledge is passed through experience and tradition, not just teaching.

items.prompt:
Read the poem below.

'Sidewalk Chalk'
I drew a house on the sidewalk,
A sun and a dog and a tree.
I put in a door that was open wide
And made it a home for me.
Then rain came and washed it away,
And I stared at the gray and the wet.
But the house I drew in my mind that day
Is one I have not forgotten yet.

What is the main idea of this poem? What does the last stanza mean?
items.answer: The main idea is that things we create with imagination stay with us even after they are gone. The child drew a chalk house that washed away in the rain, but the memory of it remained. The last stanza means that even though the physical chalk drawing is gone, the memory of it — the house the child imagined — stays in the mind and is not forgotten. Imagination creates something lasting.

steps: Read the whole poem first.
The first stanza: child draws an imaginary home in chalk.
The second stanza: rain washes it away, the child is sad.
The last two lines: the child remembers the house even after it is gone.
Main idea: imagination creates something that outlasts the physical object.
The last stanza shows memory and imagination are more permanent than chalk on a sidewalk.

items.prompt:
Read the fable below.

A rooster crowed at dawn every morning. The other animals believed his crowing made the sun rise. One morning, the rooster overslept. The sun rose anyway. 'Hmm,' said the rooster. 'The sun comes up with or without me.' He was quieter after that.

What is the moral of this fable? What detail from the story most clearly shows the moral?
items.answer: The moral is that we should not overestimate our own importance — the world does not depend on us as much as we think. The detail that most clearly shows this is that the sun rose even when the rooster overslept and did not crow. This one event proved that the rooster's crowing had nothing to do with the sunrise, even though he and the other animals believed it did.

steps: Ask: what mistake did the rooster make in his thinking?
He believed his crowing caused the sun to rise — he thought he was essential.
Key event: the rooster overslept, did not crow, and the sun rose anyway.
The rooster learns: 'The sun comes up with or without me.'
Moral: do not assume you are more important or necessary than you really are.

items.prompt:
Read the story below.

Derek had a rock collection. He kept them in a shoebox under his bed. His favorites were a smooth black stone from the beach and a sparkly piece of quartz his aunt gave him. One day his little sister got into the box. She held up the quartz. 'Pretty!' she said. Derek stared at her. Then he sat down beside her. 'That one is from Aunt Maya,' he said. 'Want me to tell you about all of them?'

What does Derek's decision to sit with his sister and tell her about the rocks tell you about his character?
items.answer: Derek's decision shows that he is patient and generous. At first he might have been upset that his sister got into his collection. But instead of scolding her, he sat down beside her and offered to share the stories behind his rocks. This shows he values sharing what he loves with others, even when it interrupts his privacy.

steps: Look at Derek's reaction when he finds his sister with his things.
He 'stared' — a moment of surprise or concern.
But he chose to sit beside her instead of getting angry.
He invites her into his world by offering to tell the stories.
This shows patience, generosity, and a caring character — he shares rather than protects.

items.prompt:
Read the poem below.

'Morning'
The rooster crows,
The dog lifts his head,
Mom calls from downstairs,
Get out of bed.
The smell of eggs
Comes drifting through,
Another day starts,
And so do you.

What is this poem about? What feeling does it give the reader?
items.answer: This poem is about the start of a regular morning. It describes the sounds and smells of waking up — a rooster, a dog, mom calling, eggs cooking. The poem gives the reader a warm, comfortable, familiar feeling. The last line ('Another day starts, and so do you') makes it feel like this is a reliable, ordinary morning — which feels safe and cozy.

steps: Read the poem and list what happens: rooster crows, dog lifts head, mom calls, smell of eggs.
All of these are morning events — the poem is about waking up.
Ask: what feeling do these details create? Warmth, familiarity, routine.
The last two lines tie it together: a new day begins for the reader too.
Feeling: cozy, safe, familiar — like any ordinary good morning.

items.prompt:
Read the story below.

The day Lily found the library was the day her life changed. She had been walking home the long way. She pushed open a heavy door and stepped inside. The air smelled like paper. Tall shelves reached the ceiling. A librarian looked up and smiled. 'First time here?' she said. Lily nodded. 'Then you have a lot of wonderful days ahead of you,' said the librarian.

What does the librarian mean when she says 'you have a lot of wonderful days ahead of you'?
items.answer: The librarian means that Lily has many great books ahead of her to read and enjoy. She is saying that discovering a library opens up a world of stories and knowledge — all the wonderful experiences that come from reading. The librarian is welcoming Lily into a new world of books.

steps: Think about what a library offers: books, stories, knowledge, imagination.
The librarian knows that for someone who has never been before, the library holds endless new books to discover.
'Wonderful days ahead' = many great reading experiences are coming.
It is a warm, encouraging thing to say to someone discovering something they will love.

items.prompt:
Read the fable below.

A young deer saw her reflection in the pool. She admired her beautiful antlers. 'My antlers are magnificent,' she said. She ran through the woods — but her antlers got caught in the branches and slowed her down. A hunter got close. She ran to an open field and her quick legs carried her to safety. She stopped and thought. 'I loved what was beautiful and scorned what was useful. I will not make that mistake again.'

What is the moral of this fable? Which part of the deer's body does the moral focus on and why?
items.answer: The moral is that usefulness matters more than beauty. The deer loved her antlers because they were beautiful, but they actually slowed her down and almost got her caught. Her legs, which she had not appreciated, were what saved her. The moral focuses on the contrast between the antlers (beautiful but unhelpful) and the legs (plain but lifesaving). The deer herself states the moral at the end.

steps: Identify the two things being compared: antlers (beautiful) and legs (useful).
Antlers: admired, but caught in branches and slowed escape.
Legs: not mentioned until needed — then they save her life.
The deer states the moral herself: she loved what was beautiful and scorned what was useful.
Moral: do not value beauty over usefulness — what helps you matters more than what looks good.

items.prompt:
Read the story below.

The old quilt on Grandma's bed had patches from old shirts, a dress, and curtains. Grandma pointed to a blue square. 'That was your grandfather's work shirt,' she said. She pointed to a yellow stripe. 'That was the curtain in the kitchen where I grew up.' Rosa traced the patterns with her finger. 'The whole quilt is a story,' she said. Grandma laughed. 'The whole quilt is a life,' she replied.

What does Grandma mean when she says 'The whole quilt is a life'?
items.answer: Grandma means that each patch of the quilt comes from something real in her life — her husband's shirt, the curtains from her childhood home. Together, the patches tell the story of her entire life. The quilt is not just a blanket; it is made of memories. 'A life' means all those years and moments sewn together into one object.

steps: Rosa says 'the quilt is a story' — Grandma goes further: it is 'a life.'
Look at the details: each patch comes from a real part of Grandma's history (husband's shirt, childhood curtains).
A 'story' is one thing; a 'life' is everything — all the years, all the people, all the memories.
Grandma means the quilt holds her whole life in fabric form.

items.prompt:
Read the poem below.

'Turtle'
He does not rush,
He does not race.
He carries his house
From place to place.
When the world gets loud
And too much to take,
He pulls himself in
For his own quiet sake.

What does this poem suggest about the turtle's way of life? What can people learn from it?
items.answer: The poem suggests that the turtle lives at his own pace and takes care of himself by retreating when the world is too much. He is not in a hurry and he carries his own shelter wherever he goes — he does not depend on a fixed place for safety. People can learn that it is okay to slow down, to take breaks from noise and stress, and to carry your sense of home and safety within yourself rather than depending on the outside world.

steps: Read the poem and look at what the turtle does: moves slowly, carries his house, retreats when overwhelmed.
These are all actions a person could also consider valuable: not rushing, being self-sufficient, taking time to be quiet.
The poem uses the turtle as a symbol for a peaceful, self-contained way of living.
Lesson for people: it is okay to slow down and retreat sometimes — taking care of yourself is wisdom, not weakness.

items.prompt:
Read the story below.

The twins, Mia and Noah, always disagreed. Mia loved the city — the noise, the buildings, the pizza places on every corner. Noah loved the country — the quiet, the fields, the sound of rain on a tin roof. One summer, they went to the country together. Noah showed Mia the stars. She had never seen so many. She said nothing, but she looked for a long time.

What does Mia's silence at the end of the story suggest about her?
items.answer: Mia's silence suggests she is surprised and moved by the stars — something she has never experienced in the city. She has always loved the city, but the stars give her something new to think about. Her long, silent look suggests the stars made an impression on her that she cannot put into words yet. She may not be ready to admit she likes something about the country, but her silence shows she is genuinely affected by what she sees.

steps: Mia is described as someone who loves the city — she is set up as the opposite of Noah.
At the end, she sees the stars for the first time.
'She said nothing, but she looked for a long time' — silence in a story means something.
When someone looks at something for a long time without speaking, they are usually deeply moved.
Inference: Mia is impressed or even a little changed by the experience, even if she will not say so.

items.prompt:
Read the fable below.

A raven saw a swan and was jealous of her beautiful white feathers. He decided that the swan was white because she lived in the water. He left his home and went to live by the river. He washed himself all day but his feathers stayed black. He searched for food in the water but he did not know how to find it. He grew thin. He had given up his home for nothing.

What is the main idea of this fable? What mistake did the raven make?
items.answer: The main idea is that trying to be someone else — or envying what others have — leads to loss. The raven's mistake was assuming the swan's white feathers came from living in water (a false assumption), and he gave up his home to copy her way of life. He lost his home and went hungry, but never got white feathers. The real mistake was envy leading to a bad decision based on a wrong belief.

steps: Identify the raven's problem: jealousy of the swan's white feathers.
Identify the false assumption: he thought the water caused the white feathers.
What happened: he gave up his home, could not find food in the water, stayed black, grew thin.
Main idea: envy makes you give up what you have to chase what you cannot get.
Moral: be content with what you are — trying to be someone else usually leads to loss.

items.prompt:
Read the story below.

Marco had never cooked before. His dad handed him a wooden spoon. 'Stir slowly,' he said. Marco stirred. The soup swirled around and around. His dad added salt. 'How do you know how much?' Marco asked. 'You taste it,' said Dad. Marco tasted. 'More?' said Dad. 'A little more,' said Marco. They ate the soup together. It tasted like something new.

What does 'it tasted like something new' mean at the end of the story?
items.answer: It means the soup tasted special because Marco had helped make it for the first time. The phrase 'something new' suggests a new experience — not just a new flavor, but a new feeling. Marco had never cooked before, and this was his first time contributing to a meal. The soup tasted new because he had helped create it, which added something beyond just the ingredients.

steps: The phrase 'tasted like something new' is not just about flavor.
Think about what was new: Marco's first time cooking, his first time contributing to a meal.
The 'new' taste is the feeling of having made something yourself.
It is a metaphor for a new experience, a new skill, and a connection with his dad.
The ending celebrates the experience of trying something for the first time.

items.prompt:
Read the poem below.

'Storm'
The sky turns green,
The wind picks up,
The dog hides under
The kitchen cup — 
No, not a cup,
A table, a chair,
The dog just hides
Under anything there.
And I sit still
With the windows shaking,
And think that the world
Is a little too loud
For my own making.

What does the speaker mean in the last four lines?
items.answer: The speaker means that the storm is so loud and intense that it feels bigger and more powerful than anything the speaker could have created or imagined. 'My own making' refers to the speaker's sense of control — the storm is beyond what they can manage or understand. The speaker feels small and overwhelmed by the storm's power, just like the dog hiding under the furniture.

steps: Read the last four lines carefully: 'And I sit still / With the windows shaking / And think that the world / Is a little too loud for my own making.'
'My own making' means what I can handle or what I created.
The world is 'too loud' = the storm is bigger than the speaker can cope with.
The speaker is overwhelmed, sitting still because there is nothing to do.
Like the dog hiding, the speaker is waiting for something too powerful to pass.

items.prompt:
Read the story below.

Every night, Aiden asked his dad the same question: 'What was the best part of your day?' His dad always had an answer. One night, Dad came home very late and very tired. Aiden was almost asleep. He heard his father sit on the edge of his bed. 'What was the best part of your day?' his dad whispered. Aiden smiled in the dark.

Why did Aiden smile in the dark when his dad asked the question?
items.answer: Aiden smiled because his dad had turned the question back on him — the same question Aiden always asked. But it also means his dad, despite being very tired, made the effort to come in and connect with Aiden before he fell asleep. Aiden smiled because the question meant his dad cares about him and their ritual, even at the end of a hard day. The smile shows warmth and love.

steps: Identify the pattern: Aiden always asks his dad 'what was the best part of your day?'
This night, the dad asks Aiden the same question.
Aiden smiles: this is surprising but also deeply touching — Dad remembered their tradition.
Despite being exhausted, Dad still took the time to come to Aiden's room.
The smile = happiness, warmth, love — Dad's effort means more than the words of the question.

items.prompt:
Read the story below.

The new student had an accent that nobody recognized. Some kids giggled. Marcus did not giggle. At lunch he walked to the new student's table. 'Where are you from?' Marcus asked. 'Nigeria,' the boy said. 'My name is Emeka.' 'I'm Marcus,' said Marcus. 'What do people eat for lunch in Nigeria?' Emeka laughed. 'Many things,' he said. 'But not this.' He poked his mashed potatoes. Marcus laughed too.

What is the main idea of this story? How does Marcus's question help the story reach its conclusion?
items.answer: The main idea is that curiosity and kindness can bridge the distance between strangers. Marcus's question — 'What do people eat for lunch in Nigeria?' — is important because it is the kind of question that shows genuine interest in someone's culture, not just politeness. It opens the door for Emeka to be funny and real, which creates the laugh they share. Instead of treating Emeka as strange, Marcus treats him as interesting. That shift from giggling (the other kids) to laughing together is the story's resolution.

steps: Main idea: curiosity and kindness can overcome the awkwardness of difference.
Marcus does not laugh at Emeka — he goes to sit with him.
His question about food is a good one: it treats Emeka's background as interesting, not weird.
Emeka responds with humor about the mashed potatoes — the question gave him space to be himself.
They laugh together: this is the moment of connection.
Marcus's curiosity is what turns a moment of otherness into a beginning of friendship.
